name: 9-Box Grid
description: Plots employees on Performance vs. Potential to inform talent decisions - who to promote, develop, or manage out.
example: An org uses the grid each year to identify its "high performance, high potential" box for accelerated leadership development, and its "low performance, low potential" box for a structured improvement plan or exit.
steps: X-axis: Performance (Low to High) — how well they are doing in their current role.
Y-axis: Potential (Low to High) — how much larger a role they could realistically grow into.
High performance + high potential: invest in accelerated development.
High performance + low potential: recognize and retain as strong specialists, not future leaders.
Low performance + high potential: coach - often a fit or ramp-up issue, not a capability ceiling.
Low performance + low potential: manage through a structured improvement plan.
when_to_use: Use it for "how would you design a talent review process" or "how should this manager think about their team" questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it as the sole input for an individual promotion/termination decision in a real organization - it is a talent-planning lens, not a complete performance review.
pitfalls: Conflating current Performance with future Potential - a strong current performer is not automatically high-potential for a very different future role.
Using it as a forced-ranking tool that pits team members against each other rather than a planning input.

name: McKinsey 7S Framework
description: A model of seven interdependent elements (Strategy, Structure, Systems, Shared Values, Skills, Style, Staff) that all need to align for an organization to work well.
example: A company adopts a new customer-centric Strategy but keeps its old hierarchical Structure and command-and-control Style - the misalignment between Strategy and the other Ss is why the transformation stalls.
steps: Strategy — the plan for building and sustaining an advantage.
Structure — how the organization is divided and coordinated.
Systems — the processes and procedures that get work done.
Shared Values — the core beliefs that shape culture (the framework's center).
Skills — the capabilities the organization and its people actually have.
Style — how leadership actually behaves, not just what they say.
Staff — the people, their roles, and how they are developed.
Identify which elements are misaligned with the intended Strategy, and which should change first to unblock the rest.
when_to_use: Use it for "why is this reorg/transformation struggling" or "assess organizational alignment" questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for a narrow individual-performance question - it is an organization-level diagnostic, not an individual one.
pitfalls: Treating the "hard" elements (Strategy, Structure, Systems) as the whole story - misalignment often actually lives in the "soft" elements (Shared Values, Style, Skills, Staff), which are easy to skip over.
Diagnosing misalignment without proposing which element should change first - not all seven can move at once.

name: OKR Framework (Objectives & Key Results)
description: A goal-setting methodology popularized by Intel and Google connecting ambitious qualitative Objectives to 3-5 quantitative, measurable Key Results.
example: Objective: Transform customer support into a competitive retention advantage. KR 1: Reduce average first-response time from 4 hours to under 15 minutes. KR 2: Achieve CSAT rating > 92%. KR 3: Automate 40% of tier-1 repetitive inquiries via AI agent.
steps: Define the Objective (O): Qualitative, inspirational, time-bound statement of what is to be accomplished (e.g. 'Build the most reliable checkout engine in Southeast Asia').
Set Key Results (KRs): 3 to 5 quantitative metrics that prove the objective was met (e.g. 'Reduce payment gateway failure rate from 4.2% to < 0.5%').
Keep KRs Outcome-Based: Measure business and user outcomes, not task activities or to-do lists.
Target Ambition (Stretch Goals): Target a 70% achievement rate (a score of 0.7 is successful; 1.0 means the goal was too easy).
Cascade and Align: Bi-directional goal alignment where 50% of OKRs are set top-down and 50% bottom-up across teams.
when_to_use: Use for company-wide, department, and team quarterly alignment, performance management, and strategy execution.
when_not_to_use: Do not use OKRs as a rigid 1:1 formula for compensation and bonuses (that encourages sandbagging and low ambition).
pitfalls: Writing Key Results as tasks (e.g. 'Launch feature X') instead of metric outcomes (e.g. 'Increase conversion rate by 15%').
Setting too many OKRs (more than 3-5 per team causes loss of focus).
